utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp will now conclude his re-examination of you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Peraj. The last area I want to cull with you in respect to the MUP is something you said in cross-examination when you said that you saw when houses near the bus station were being torched and the regular police were there and stood by. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1999. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the month?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could it have been before the 25th of March, 1999, or was it after?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was March. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you recall if it was before or after the NATO campaign started?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the NATO campaign. It was, in fact, during those days that the NATO air-strike started, but the NATO air-strikes started later. It was after these houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that the regular police were present and stood by. What do you mean by regular police? Which armed police organisation were they attached to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the uniforms they were wearing and their outer appearance, they were regular police of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said when -- you said when you tried to intervene to stop this, the commander told you to mind your own business and prevented you from stopping the persons burning down the people's houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to the guards that were there, close to me was my commander, Milos Djosan, and I told him that we have to intervene because the fire is very close. He said to mind my own business. This is nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, it was Milos Djosan who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My commander, not the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the -- to the VJ. You were asked about the time when General Ojdanic was appointed, and you said it was in 1997 and he succeeded General Perisic. Can I just refer briefly to a part of your last statement and ask you a question that arises, and this is from paragraph 100. "I listened to an address by Perisic during a meeting held at the end of May/beginning of June 1998 in the military club, in the military barracks in Pristina." At that meeting in June 1998, or May 1998, was General Perisic still the commander -- still the Chief of Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So General Ojdanic would have succeeded him subsequent to that, naturally?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to the VJ, you said that before 1998 they did not destroy whole villages. And you said further in 1998 the village of Kavez [phoen] was destroyed and other villages. Can you recall the other villages that were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Kavez, I don't think that name exists or maybe you pronounced it wrong. I don't know which village you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Just tell us which villages, if you can recall, were destroyed by the VJ in 1998.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They shelled several villages in the vicinity of Komorane, where they said that there were members of the KLA there. They had their bases, so KLA bases were in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, you were asked about an informal meeting, and this was the informal meeting in which Stojanovic -- right, Stojanovic said houses should be burned and at least 100 persons should -- should be killed. And you were asked -- or it was suggested that this discussion involved a group of local people. What I want to ask you is this: Can you remember who among the group said that we needed authorisation for that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Stojanovic was speaking like this to Micunovic and Kovacevic, he said: An operation has to be undertaken to burn the houses to ashes and a hundred -- at least a hundred heads should go. I explained the reason yesterday why I thought they said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Peraj, is: Who uttered these words: At least a hundred heads should go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after that somebody, according to you, said that: We need authorisation for that. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And then someone said: I will arrange that with Pavkovic. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you went to the Pastriku Hotel under the command of -- or at --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the paramilitaries who were there told you to go and speak to their boss. Did they tell you who their boss was?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, may it please, that is the re-examination for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what is the paragraph that deals with the hundred heads must go?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I mean, my note of yesterday, obviously we'll need to review this in particular, but the person, according to the witness yesterday, who would -- said he would contact Pavkovic was Kovacevic. That -- is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My recollection was that he was asked a question in which people were lumped together and it was a compound question, so I did not know who said what. And there was a group of people that was asked about. So I just thought I would just make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, having said that I also noted that answer in regard to paragraph 62, so obviously we'll need to review the transcript on that. Now, Mr. Stamp - and this is addressed to everyone - the various documents which have been referred to at some stage in the evidence and have been used as part of the evidence are admitted. Those that haven't been translated, subject, obviously, to translation and therefore marked for identification until that happens, when they're translated it's for the party presenting the document to inform the Trial Chamber about the translation in a written filing so that we can take account of the position and deal with any further matters that require to be specifically confirmed so far as admission is concerned. Two documents were referred to but actually were not used, although you'll see mention of them in the transcript, and that's 6D34 and 35 in the course of Mr. Lukic's cross-examination. So they do not appear to me to have formed any part of the procedure -- the proceedings. And one document I want to ask you about, Mr. Stamp. 3D60 is the notes that were taken of the telephone conversation or the telephone interview with Mr. Peraj. Now, that was used only in cross-examination by Mr. Visnjic. Is your position that it's part of the process so far as the Defence want it to be, or have you a position that we should take account of all that's in that document? Because I don't think it's been tendered as part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I think the Defence wanted to use it for cross-examination purposes and the witness was not -- the witness accepted what was put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So we confine our consideration of it to the purpose for which it was used in the course of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the event that you actually wish to clarify that matter you raised, it's transcript -- yesterday's transcript page 58, beginning at line 14. He said: "It was the person who was with Kovacevic who said we need authorisation for that." And the other fellow said: "I'll arrange with Pavkovic." That's the testimony from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just make one suggestion, with your permission. Having regard to what you said yesterday about the Defence or parties getting translations for only the relevant parts of long documents, which is a completely reasonable position, can I ask, however, though, that the front page which might give a general description of what the document is about be translated and the last page with the signature, the person who signed it, just at least the signature block and what is said about that commandant or position wrote also be included in the translation, plus the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I mean, that's a very reasonable comment, but I don't think it's possible to legislate for it. Mr. Stamp's given an example of when it would be helpful to have parts of the front and last page of a document also translated, albeit only a small part of it is necessary for the case. But I think as a matter of exercising a wise discretion when it comes to deciding what you invite the translators to actually translate bearing that comment in mind. Well, Mr. Peraj, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish you all the best, all the people here in this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Parties are naturally anxious to have as much clarification about the sitting arrangements of the Bench as possible, and I can give some guidance on that. The sitting programme for August and September can be seen in the Tribunal web site and should by now be brought up-to-date to reflect the consideration of particular arrangements that had to be made. In the immediate future, it is unlikely that this case will proceed on the 29th of August because the court is required for an appeal hearing. If, of course, that's cancelled for any reason then the situation will change. That hearing was initially also scheduled for the 30th of August, but that's been changed. It's no longer scheduled for the 30th, so we will be sitting then. We shall not be sitting on the first Monday of September, which is I think the 4th, and we shall not be sitting on Monday, the 23rd of October, not on the 24th which is a public holiday, but in addition to that we will not be sitting on Monday, the 23rd, with a view to giving as long a weekend as possible in these circumstances. And we shall not be sitting the first week of October. That will be one of the discretionary recess weeks that the Chamber can take. I appreciate there's some concern about the frequency with which the trial will be sitting on both Friday afternoons and Monday mornings, thus curtailing the weekend. There's been a modification of that to some extent, and you'll see the Fridays on which we're sitting in the morning reflected in the web site. Basically this Trial Chamber will sit on a Friday morning if possible, but the demands of other trials prevent that frequently. So unfortunately our primary slot is Friday afternoon, but I am as interested and indeed the other Judges are as interested as you are in moving that to Friday morning. So we'll keep our eye on the opportunities arising for that. So that's as much of an indication as I can give you at the moment of what the future holds so far as sitting arrangements are concerned. That takes me, Mr. Hannis, to your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we call in the next witness I'd like to make a brief oral application. The Defence has filed a response to our second 92 bis motion concerning a protected witness from an international humanitarian organisation. We would like to ask leave to file a reply to that motion and ask if we could have until a week from Friday, that is the 25th of August, in which to file that reply. They have agreed for now that he could come without cross-examination, but they have an objection to a portion of some of the materials attached to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that the timing you suggest fits in with when you envisage that evidence being presented to the Court? It's -- I mean, context is important here. If -- I appreciate it's -- you're endeavouring not to bring the witness, but it's quite nice to have the material in the context of an appropriate stage. And you're satisfied that this is evidence for much later in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is evidence that would come in much later in the case, but the issues regarding its admissibility or whether or not it should come in sort of relate to some of the issues that relate to As Seen, As Told and Under Orders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay. The second point I have for you is the reply that you've -- you have -- or the response you have from the Defence, is that a joint response?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who is the lead counsel in that; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's Ojdanic, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan is being fingered.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It was prepared jointly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you tend to be the spokesman when another one can't be identified. Are you happy that there should be a further reply from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the time-scale is gives you no problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That application will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Your Honour, Ms. Carter will call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court, we now call the Prosecution witness, Xhevahire Rrahmani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now just give me a moment before you go for the next witness. Does any part of your examination of this witness require a private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. It is conceivable, though, that cross-examination may, depends on the issues arising. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It is quite possible, Your Honour. There is a protected witness that is -- that could come in issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking also of the nature of part of the allegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the conduct described. I flag that up for Defence counsel, that there are two issues there. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it's because I've come late, but I'm not aware of a protected witness that may be in issue, and so I could inadvertently get into it without being aware. So maybe that should be made -- I should know about that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, information on this can be exchanged informally. It doesn't need to be dealt with -- I take it that you can relay a message to Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to deal with that. And as far as the nature of the conduct is concerned, then it may not be an issue in the case. I don't know. But if it is, then I expect you to alert me to your intention to cross-examine the witness on that. Very well. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we have the earphones, please, first of all, so that ... Ms. Rrahmani, would you now make the solemn declaration by reading out loud the document which is placed in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. We have before us a copy of a statement that's been given to us setting out your account of various things, but it's part of the procedure we follow here that witnesses generally come to court to be asked further questions about these events and perhaps about other matters. And that's what we're about to hear now. So a number of people will ask you questions, some of them you might find are difficult, in which case you can explain that to us. Or if you don't know the answer, you should tell us. And some of them may involve a challenge to your evidence. You should be clear before you start that it's part of the system under which this Tribunal operates that questions challenging the evidence of a witness are often asked. So please don't be surprised when that happens. And if we think that anyone is asking you a question which is improper, then we will intervene to prevent that happening. The first person to ask you questions will be on behalf of the Prosecutor, and that's Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For ease of the witness as well as the Court, I prepared a hard copy of her statement and I ask that that be delivered to the witness. And while that's taking place, we would request that the 92 bis package be placed upon the screen. That's e-court number P02239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the hard copy you've presented to her in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. We've still to get the -- when you say "on the screen," you mean on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this 92 bis package is, in fact, in Albanian. The linked documents to it include an English as well as a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, we now have the English on our screen, I think. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, will you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Xhevahire Rrahmani.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, you have a hard copy of your statement in front of you. Have you had an opportunity to look over that statement previously?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is the document that you have in front of you the same statement that you believe you've reviewed before?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based upon your review, do you find the statement to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request at this time that the statement be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as you know, the practice we've been following is that in the absence of objection that will automatically happen, and therefore this is tendered by you and will be part of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In addition, this witness has been called pursuant to 92 bis (D). We're also requesting the tendering of e-court number P02240, which is the transcript from the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I regret I overlooked that because it wasn't given to me as part of the set of documents, but I'm sure we'll get a copy later on in the course of the evidence, so carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same applies so far as the transcript is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, I'm now going to ask you questions in regards to your statement to both expand as well as to clarify certain aspects, and the first topics that we will cover is going to be your deportation or displacement throughout Kosovo. We will later deal with the incident that took place in the barn in Cirez. I would like to direct you first to approximately March 24th, 1999. Where were you residing at that time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Before the 24th of March, on the 22nd of February I left my home and I went to live in Vushtrri at Naim Muzaci's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why did you leave to live in Naim Muzaci's house?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because the army was in the mountains of Taraxh and they were shelling and our children were scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "the army," can you describe who was shelling those villages?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you able to see these forces or is this something that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We heard from other people, but we heard the shots also, and there were bullets that came up to my house in my courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At what time was -- were the bullets in your courtyard?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It was at 2.00 p.m. While two days after that my husband and my brother-in-law, Bajram, they were told by the army to leave the house because otherwise they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was the date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We left on the 22nd. The other one was on the 24th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At any time did you return back to your village of Bukos in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. We returned three or four days later, and I went myself to the courtyard -- to the gates of my house, as we call them, and the army did not allow me to get into my own house. I saw the Serbian army, a tractor, and another tractor with a trailer loading everything that I had in my house, a television, everything, my furniture, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, you stood up during that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want our learned friend from the other side to point out in the statement where we can find this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I doubt if it's there. I assume it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. It is not in the statement. The statement begins approximately March 26th. These events occur prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We just wanted to have this on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you should have a statement of the witness that does cover that period, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why has a statement of these events not been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There is no statement -- this was first learned in proofing on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why didn't you disclose the proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time no proofing notes were created. As this witness has been taken under 92 bis (D) and as this portion of the evidence will be taken live, no additional submissions were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's disappointing. If you obtain additional information in the form of a statement when you're preparing a witness to give evidence, I would have thought it was common courtesy, apart from your obligation under the general practice of the Tribunal, to disclose the content of that additional evidence to the Defence so that they could be prepared for it. Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, as this is taken live -- as live testimony, the witness should be able to expand upon the evidence that she's given. It's fairly clear from the statement itself that it indicates certain activities took place within her family and within her home that caused her to leave her village. We're just clarifying that portion which begins in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is leaving another village before she ever gets to the village that the statement begins at. It's events in a completely different location from those that are already in the statement. Now, your argument that because it's viva voce live evidence in court I don't follow. That would suggest that if the Prosecution could carry out its investigations with a photographic memory, they would never need to disclose anything. Now, that can't possibly be right. In fact, it just sounds preposterous to me. So do you or do you not concede that this should have been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it should have been disclosed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now. Well, you're very fortunate that nobody's taking issue -- well, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I happen to be the person first up for cross-examination, and I think that the proofing notes should be disclosed to me before I am required to proceed with that. This may be the beginning of a number of things that are in the proofing notes that we don't know about. I don't know how much more this is going to happen, but basically her entire testimony since she started deals with matters that are not in her statement and apparently are contained in proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't rise while you were putting your questions to the Prosecution, but if this is an attempt -- if it's an attempt or oversight, it does nonetheless circumvent the disclosure obligation under Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems clear. The -- the Trial Chamber actually contemplated in making an order when we issued our brief order about procedure at the beginning of the trial including something about this, but we thought that things were progressing well between the parties so far as disclosure was concerned and didn't think it was necessary to do so. And indeed, the Defence's attitude recently has been that the Prosecution has been very cooperative in this case, and therefore -- even when they feel things have gone wrong, they don't seem to be anxious to press the matter to sanction but simply to have it recorded, just in case there's an accumulation of these events. But this is something that we should probably say a little more about at this stage to avoid any repetition, so please give the Bench a moment to deliberate on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we think it right to make an order here and now on the Prosecution requiring them to disclose to the Defence immediately any additional information they obtain from witnesses who are to be led in the trial. And that's such an all-encompassing requirement that it covers obviously both incriminatory evidence and exculpatory evidence. So anything material that you learn in the course of proofing must be disclosed forthwith to the Defence. Now, in this instance all the Defence require of you is that prior to the cross-examination the additional information is disclosed, and I hope you can make arrangements for that while your own examination is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And respectfully, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits this became a confusion over what is deemed to be new and different and what is deemed to be clarification of a prior statement. This witness in approximately a sentence and a half will get to paragraph 2 beginning the statement. It was not the intention of the Prosecution to go outside the scope of the statement or to lead to any sort of surprise on Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've got evidence of shelling by the VJ in the mountains which you then interpreted as shelling of villages, although the witness didn't say that. It's pretty significant stuff which relates to an area which is not currently -- or at least a place which is not currently covered I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in the statement. So I doubt if there's any question but that this material should have been disclosed. However, we are relieved to know that we can proceed very quickly to material of which the Defence have notice. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make the observation with regard to the statement just made by my learned friend from Texas that this is a great deal more than just a clarification. Now, I'm willing to accept that it was an oversight that it was not delivered to us, but it's -- that's not an explanation, that is just a clarification. Because it goes into a brand new matter that's not in the statement. It's not clarifying anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think all you're doing is repeating what I've said, Mr. Ackerman. So please continue, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, I'd like to focus you beginning on March 24th, 1999. Where were you residing on that date?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In Vushtrri at my son-in-law Naim Muzaci.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And at what point did you leave that location?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: On the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where did you go on March 26th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We went to the village of Kozica, to my husband's uncle, Xhemajl Xhema. He is from the municipality of Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why did you go to Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because they were shelling in Vushtrri and we were scared about our children's safety. So that's why we went to Kozica. We could not go to our house because there were -- the army was there, so we went to Kozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your travelling between these two villages, did you encounter any sort of Serbian military or police unit?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. They were in the village of Taraxh but we did not go that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some point in time soldiers entered a house and there were approximately 30 soldiers. Where was this house?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In the village of Kozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in the village of Kozica, can you please describe the soldiers that you saw.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In the village Cirez there were there some soldiers, but after three days they came to Kozica. In the beginning they shelled, but then they came there with trucks and other vehicles. There were people who were killed. Ten people were killed, and three people were injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I -- where we were, there were many women and children in the courtyard of Rrahim's house. And the shells fell on the courtyard, and ten people were killed and three were injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who was doing the shelling that resulted in these injuries?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The Serbian army shelled from Cirez to the village of Kozica, in the courtyard of Rrahim. I don't know his surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see any of these Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: When the infantry came there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did the infantry look like?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They had green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: These uniforms, were they solid? Did they have a pattern? Do you have any other detail about the green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Green uniforms. They had ribbon in the upper arm, but I had my children there and I saw the people who were killed and injured. So I wasn't, you know, paying too much attention whether they -- what they were wearing. So I just saw that the uniform was green, and they had a red ribbon in the upper arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I understand there was quite a bit of confusion at that time, but are you able to tell us if they were solid green uniforms or camouflage green uniforms or some other pattern?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were just green. It was regular army, and I'm not very sure about this. That was the first time I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After this incident took place where these soldiers gathered within the courtyard, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We were told to sit down. Nobody should stand. We sat down. They came very close to us, and the people who were injured, they were trying to dress their wounds. They injured them and they now were dressing their wounds. We left the dead people where they were and we moved away from them because we were scared. There was a young man among us, 28, 30 years old. He was I think mentally disabled, and he was shouting and crying. He was eating a boiled egg, I think. And because he was shouting and crying, they shot him immediately, right there and then, in the Kozica village, in Rrahim's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When the infantry entered this village, had there previously been any sort of fighting or any sort of armed combat within the village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, but they were shooting towards the Kozica village, it's in Cicavica. In the village of Kozica, they shelled several houses. So all the women with the children -- because we were all scared and feared for our lives, we went to Rrahim's courtyard. There were 300 of us more or less, and after the shelling stopped the infantry left. After they killed that young man, they took petrol or something and burnt the houses. They just left one -- what we call oda, which is a guestroom, so they burned his whole house just -- they left -- they spared this oda, the guestroom. They left that room alone because they wanted to get all our valuables, whatever we had, rings and earrings, necklaces, and all our IDs, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The individuals who were doing the burning as well as the shooting, were these the same infantrymen that you had referred to previously?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, they were infantry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some point in time did you leave Kozica village and go some place else?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. After they searched us, they told us to go to Skenderaj because fighting -- there's fighting here. The infantry has to go to Cicavica, so you need to go to a place where there's no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you see fighting or hear fighting at that time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. We were told to leave for Skenderaj immediately. They were following us all the time, watching us whether we were going to Skenderaj or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The persons who were watching you, are they the same infantrymen or are they additional soldiers or police?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The same soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long did they follow you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Well, two hours. It was two hours, because it's 8 kilometres from Kozica to Skenderaj, so -- I'm telling you approximately because I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When they were following you, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They were on trucks, and they were laughing at us. They were saying something to us, but I don't know the language so I could not tell you what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Skenderaj, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Before entering Skenderaj, there was a police check-point, Serbian police check-point. They did not allow us to get into Skenderaj. That night we stayed in a meadow which was called Lah Tushila [phoen] service. It's before you get into Skenderaj itself. Myself, my children, the whole group slept on that meadow, and the children were suffering because they were starving and they did not -- they were very thirsty.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let me back up for just a moment. You indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that horrifies me, that comment, Ms. Carter, "back up." We're still on page 1 of this statement. What was the purpose of having a statement in the case of this witness if we're just going to explore it all in even greater detail in oral examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point we're attempting to describe for the Court who specifically was engaged during the time of this woman's deportation through Kosovo. What is not clear from the statement is specifically which forces, what the uniforms looked like. As it's become a great issue, given the fact it is both military, politicians, as well as the police that are involved in this case, we want the Court to be very clear who was active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean it's become a great issue? It has been an issue since 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And this witness is just attempting to describe for the Court who was engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is this not explored in detail when the statements are taken for the purpose of presentation in court?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as before, the statement was taken in the year 2000. I cannot speak to you about what was taking place at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I imagine that's right. I, yet again, pose the question which will never be answered, I suspect, as to why these statements aren't updated long before we get to the trial stage so that we can get on with the job we're required to do in the context of evidence that we can quickly read and allow to be challenged in court. As it is, this -- spending this time on the detail of these events with this type of statement in front of us is really not making progress at all in the trial. It's very disappointing that we have to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, when you were at the check-point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there something substantive to be said, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. I think this has turned into -- I mean, you have made some observation about it yourself. But if you look at the Rule 92 bis itself, it provides for evidence to be offered in lieu of testimony. And what's going on here is a complete viva voce presentation of this witness's testimony. It's not a 92 bis proceeding. We were informed that this was a 92 bis witness and that her testimony on direct would be her 92 bis statement, and we were given her 92 bis statement in that regard and our examinations, cross-examinations were prepared with that in mind. We come into court with no notice at all, no indication at all, no proofing notes at all, nothing, that this witness was turned into a viva voce witness. And now incredible amounts of testimony are coming in that have nothing to do with her statement, not contained in her statement, or anything else. I think it's extraordinarily unfair. It violates the rule of 92 bis. If they want to have a 92 bis witness, then that's what they have. If they want to have a viva voce witness, then that's what they have. But they can't have -- can't say they're having one and then have the other. And it's now become a matter where I wouldn't -- I'd hesitate to try to do a cross-examination with so much new material going into the transcript without having time to go through that transcript and compare it with what I've already prepared. So I think it's unfair, and I think it should not happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman has received a notification from the Office of the Prosecution that indicated this witness would be anticipated to have one hour live testimony. In addition, this Court has already previously addressed the 92 bis witnesses, to have clarification made as live testimony here in court. It is unfortunate that Mr. Ackerman was not able to be present during those conversations, but this witness is being handled within the rulings of the Court previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you tell me that this will last one hour, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is my anticipation, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that still your anticipation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, subtracting time for discussions as well as objections, yes, we still anticipate that the Prosecution's portion of this witness will take one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, as Mr. Ackerman also knows, Rule 92 bis provides that the evidence may be given in writing under that Rule in whole or in part, and while that, generally speaking, envisages a clearly divided testimony in which it's easy to identify the written and the oral, this sort of thing is not excluded by 92 bis so far as clarification is necessary. So what we shall do is monitor the progress of this examination, bearing in mind the submissions that have been made. And we shall decide at the end of the examination-in-chief, if we reach that, whether we consider this as an appropriate way for future witnesses to be led. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated that there was a police check-point that stopped you from going on to Skenderaj. Can you please describe for us who was manning the check-point?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was a policeman who came out and told us not to get in Skenderaj. We saw tanks. There was a room inside, 4 by 4 metres I think, but only -- I don't know whether there were policemen inside there, but this policeman came out, and he said that we could not enter Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the policeman.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you speak at all to his uniform, such as colour, pattern, or any other demarcations?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did you know it was a policeman as opposed to some other person, be it citizen -- civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because he looked like a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What about him looked like a policeman?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because the soldiers we had seen before had a different uniform, and the women were saying that this is not a soldier, it's a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were in the field with your family, were there any persons, be it military or police, who were near you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. Well, they stayed there all night, but they did not come close to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who stayed there all night?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The Serbian army, but they did not come close to us. And they did not say anything to us. We stayed there in the field, the children were sleeping, some women were even breast-feeding. We spent the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some point you left the field. Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because the same policeman said: Go away from here. Go to Gllogoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you went to Gllogoc, were there any police or military along that line?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: On the way, yes, they were on trucks and tanks, but they did not say anything to us. Close to Gllogoc, they said that the KLA had killed someone. They took Hashim Zani [phoen] from the village of Polac, municipality of Skenderaj. I think his body was found a year ago, but I don't know where. But it was there that they took him, this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I need you to back up for just a moment. You indicated that when you were on the road you saw people on tractors and other vehicles. Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I said "trucks." It was the Serbian army going back and forth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were not on tractors. And you could see only women and children. There were no men, because if they found men there, they would kill them immediately. Even young boys, 13 years old, they would kill them. I told you about that 28-year-old man who was mentally disabled, and they killed him because he was shouting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Ten days. I stayed in Gllogoc ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your time in Gllogoc, were you left in peace or did you have other involvement with the military or police?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. During those ten days we didn't have any problems. We could go out to get bread, but we didn't dare to go out to get anything else. But I have to say they did not come into the house. But because we did not have any bread anymore and we did not have any money left to buy bread, so we tried to go to Kozica to get some food for the children especially.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you went into Kozica, did you see any forces within that village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, not in Kozica, but the houses were totally burned. But in the village Cirez they were still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who did you see in the village of Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The soldiers, the same soldiers that shelled us and killed us, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: These soldiers, are these the same infantrymen that you indicated had solid green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Approximately when did you see the shelling continuing in Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: That day we were at the house of Xhemajl, but before 7.00 we went to Daka's house because it was raining. For three nights we stayed there. During the day, we went to a valley close to Tresnjos [phoen] village, municipality of Skenderaj. But that day because it was raining we went to the house of Xhafer Daka close to Cicavica, because we didn't want to be close to the soldiers, to fall into their hands, because we were afraid what they might do to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Approximately what date was this?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I'm sorry. It was in April, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some point in time you indicate in your statement that you were taken into the village of Cirez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. The infantry came. We were in Daka's house. They -- they shot a young man called Fatlum. They were shooting all the time but we did not leave the house. They were shooting outside. This young boy, Fatlum, was sent to us to tell us to leave or come to -- to go to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the witness did not say they shot a young man, but they sent a young boy, a young man.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you're saying "they," are you still referring to these same solid green infantry uniforms, or are you indicating another group?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I think it was soldiers with uniforms, dark brown and black.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In Kozica, what were the uniforms that you saw?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was a large group in plain green uniforms, others in dark brown and black uniforms. Those who took us from Daka's house had a different uniform. Those who stayed with us in Abedin's house, they had green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms of the people who took you from Kozica to Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It was green. Three of them accompanied us to the Cirez village. We stayed there for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "green," are you referring to solid green, camouflage green, or some other pattern?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Those who came to get us from Daka's house, they had camouflage uniforms, while the others, there were about 30 of them, their uniforms were plain green.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you see any interaction between the people in solid green uniforms and the people in green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, when they handed us over they discussed things with each other. I think they had discussed things before. They were expecting us because it was something like handing over people and they had agreed before, beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the soldiers who were talking together while they were in Kozica, or are you talking about soldiers who were speaking amongst each other in Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The soldiers who took us from Kozica to Cirez, I think they had agreed beforehand with the soldiers who were in the school in Cirez because when we got there, the soldiers came out of the school and they talked amongst each other. So the soldiers who accompanied us returned to Kozica and left us in the hands of the ones in Cirez.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To be clear, within your statement, are you telling us that the green camouflage persons who took you into Cirez spoke with the individuals who had black and brown uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were left with the people who were in the black and brown uniforms, how long did you stay with them?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They took us to this barn when the soldiers left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, where is it the witness says that the soldiers at Cirez had black and brown uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be on the English page 4, approximately paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, in the -- in the transcript. You say that: Are you telling us that the green camouflaged persons who took you into Cirez spoke with the individuals who had black and brown uniforms. Now, where do I see that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At approximately -- approximately page 31, and she begins to speak about the black and brown uniforms on line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On 31?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes. 5 and 6 she begins to discuss the brown and black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but these are the people who were -- who came after the boy Fatlum LNU arrived. And they're described in the statement as having green camouflage uniforms, some dark green and some light green, and in her oral evidence I've understood her to change hat to say dark brown and black.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will certainly clarify with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that not what that part says? Just go to line 5. There was a large group in plain green uniforms and others in brown and black. Those who took us from Daka's house had different uniforms. Those who stayed with us in Abedin's house, they had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding from the testimony what she was indicating is that there were solid green uniforms within the village. The green camouflage uniforms are who picked her up and took her to Cirez. Once she gets to Cirez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please don't tell the witness all that you expect to her to tell you yet again. I'm just trying to clarify the meaning of what she's already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And on page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't want your summary of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And on page 31 beginning at line 9 is when it indicates -- I said question her: Can you describe the uniforms of the people who took you from Kozica to Cirez? And that point she indicates: It was green, three of them accompanied us to Cirez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, my question related to the witnesses who took her there. Anyway, carry on. I'm delighted that you think that this is clarifying the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, what uniforms were the people wearing who took you from Kozica to Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Those who took us from Kozica to Cirez were wearing green uniforms. First, those who came to pick us up from Daka's home were wearing brown to black uniforms, whereas the other ones that I mentioned who brought us to Cirez were wearing green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where were the people -- what village were the people who wore the black and brown uniforms in?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from, because they were not deployed in Kozhice.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you meet the people in brown and black uniforms in Kozica or in Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I saw those people for the first time in Kozhice that day when they took us from Daka's home, and then after that we saw them in Cirez village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did the black and brown people arrive in Kozica and stay there with you the entire time, or did they arrive in Kozica and you later encountered them?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Only when they came to take us, and then we didn't see them anymore in Kozhice. We saw only those people with green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In Kozhice, did you see any conversation taking place with the people in green camouflage uniforms and those in black and brown camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They put us into that home, and I don't know what they discussed among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you see any interaction whatsoever between the individuals in green camouflage uniforms and those in black and brown camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, we saw them. We stayed there for three days. They came that day, one soldier came, with a woman called Mirdita. She spoke the language and she told us that we were supposed to go to Cirez. We were two groups there. On the second floor were those from Klina, Skenderaj municipality, and those from Kozhice. On the first level was I and my kids.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to stop you right here and I just need you to be very clear. Once you get to Cirez, what type of soldiers did you see there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The colour was brown and black. This is how I remember that. Because to tell you the truth, I didn't dare look at them to see what they were wearing. We just wanted to get away from them; that was our main concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long were you with - "you" collectively, meaning you and the other individuals who were brought to Cirez - how long were you with the men in brown and black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Some two hours or even more I would say, until they checked all of us, took away our girls and our mothers and whom we never saw alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We will cover that in a moment, but I need you to back up and just indicate after the two hours in Cirez with the men in the black and brown uniforms, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They kept us in that barn and told us to go again to Durmishi's house, where we were before, and they told us to leave the barn one by one and never to turn our heads back; otherwise, they said: We are going to shoot you. So we didn't dare look behind, didn't dare ask them: What happened to my mother, or to those girls that they took away, eight people that they took away from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On your way back to Kozica village, did you go by yourself or were there other soldiers or police involved?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, we went there ourselves, because this is what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where in the statement is this movement from Kozica to Cirez, this particular one referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Paragraph 17, the English page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't have paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, Your Honour. That would be on the fourth page of the English statement, the sixth full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not much later than what we're talking about just now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, we're back now to what I've numbered -- I've written my own numbers in, it's paragraph 12, it's the last paragraph on page 3. We're past that stage, are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We have now -- the -- the statement goes from paragraph -- or I'm sorry, page 4, where it indicates she goes into Cirez. You wait until page 7 before you see them come back from Cirez. As I'm trying to attempt to elicit the information with regards to who was on the transportation lines, I have skipped over the portion where she is in the barn and attempting to just give you the first portion. I will then come back to deal with the barn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But have we missed -- you've asked no questions about the first five paragraphs on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I've -- the statement appeared to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've wrongly got the impression that there was a relationship between soldiers coming for them when Fatlum LNU warned them and then going to Cirez. I thought the two were directly related from the way in which this evidence was being led. But you tell me that there's no relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the young boy speaks with them, that is between two houses within the same village. It is not a transport between two separate villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And then it says: "Immediately after that we went towards Abedin Durmishi's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's again in Kozica village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've missed all -- that's all happened before they're collected and taken to Cirez?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we're about to have a break just now then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now and we'll resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Before we begin with the witness, I wanted to make the Court aware that the proofing notes have been typed up and have already been e-mailed to Defence counsel for their review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful. But just for the avoidance of any doubt you know it's not necessarily the notes that have to be disclosed, you know that it's the material contained in them that is material obtained from the witness that has to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think that's what the order made clear at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that it's been e-mailed to me, there's almost nothing I can do with that because I can't print it here in the courtroom, and I can't follow the trial and read the e-mail at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is must be possible to print in the courtroom, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I haven't -- if it is, I haven't learned that in my minimal training.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, we were unable to print off the printer that's between on our bench as well. However, we will provide hard copies as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. If you e-mail it then to Mr. Sabbah, he will print it for you, and that will let the Prosecution concentrate on their examination, so let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, you indicated that when you arrived back into Kozica you saw military. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Return from where?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you returned from Cirez back to Kozica, did you see military in Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. Before we went to the house of Durmishi, I saw the soldiers who accompanied us to Cirez.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The soldier, correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In addition to the soldier who you saw that escorted you to Cirez, did you see other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. There were in the houses there. But I recognised the one who escorted us to Cirez. And I told the people in my group: This is the soldier that accompanied us to Cirez. And then he saw us saying something about him and then he went inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, how long were you in Kozica at that time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: When we returned from Cirez to Kozhice, before they sent us to Kozhice for three days. Then after Cirez for three, four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the three or four hours in Kozica, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: To the house of Durmishi, to that group that remained there on the second floor. We stayed for three, four hours on the first floor, and then again they sent us back to Cirez.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you went back to Cirez the second time, did you go unaccompanied or did soldiers accompany you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They accompanied us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the uniforms of the people who accompanied you back to Cirez?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I'm saying -- I'm using the word "yellow," but in fact I mean green, but we say "yellow" for green.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So the men in the green uniforms took you back to Cirez. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, two soldiers sent us back to Cirez, but they didn't stay close to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Carter, which paragraph are we on now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would be the English page 7, B/C/S page 8, Albanian page 10, and the paragraph would be the second from the bottom. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I have to say it was not at all clear to me we had advanced as far through the statement. The presentation of this evidence is not achieving any effect on me. I'm at a loss, generally speaking, as to where we've been -- which parts we've been dealing with in the statement as we go through the oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the clarification of the Court, we've passed from page 4 to page 7. Page 4 through 7 is what involves the incident in the barn. As the Court clearly appeared that they were concerned about her testifying to that in open session, I have foregone that information at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, when you returned back to the village of Cirez and you said two soldiers accompanied you, were they in solid green uniforms or in camouflage green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It was solid green.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you were in the village of Cirez, how long did you stay the second time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: For the second time we stayed three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: While you were in the village of Cirez for those three weeks, were soldiers present in the village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: While the soldiers were in the village, did they at any time take a statement from you or have you show them the barn in which your tragedy occurred?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. Before we went to the house, they placed us -- I told them that this is the barn where they took away the mother and the girls. And they told me: Go ahead, go ahead, we know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At any time did you see any sort of follow-up investigation by the soldiers who were in Cirez regarding your mother?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the three weeks in Cirez, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They told us that: You will go to Gllogoc. We will send you to Macedonia. There is no place for you here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were on the route to Glogovac, did anybody go with you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There were many people there, but nobody accompanied us. We saw trucks and lorries driving past the street, but no one specifically escorted us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you feel you had a choice whether you were to leave or not?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No one maltreated us. They just told us to go to Gllogoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I respectfully pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Carter. Mr. Ackerman -- sorry, just before you start, there is one thing I think we should clarify. The evidence of this witness insofar as it is in writing, Ms. Carter, is tendered under which rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that deals with the transcript. What about the statement that we have?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is our reading of 92 bis (D) that as this statement was entered within the transcript that it becomes part and parcel of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how is that dealt with in the transcript? Can you take me to the page in the transcript where it's dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be on page 4582 of the transcript, specifically line 12. And, Your Honour, the registrar gave the exhibit exhibit number 141 on page 4583 at lines 15 and 16 in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you tendered exhibit P2239 and called it the 92 bis package, that didn't include the transcript, because you gave it a different number?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how do these tie together when you say the statement includes -- is included in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as this witness was submitted under 92 bis (D) applying the transcript was a portion of her 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now it's no longer part of the package. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, also due to the e-court system, we were not able to take both of these documents and put them together under one e-court number, thus they were given two separate numbers, but they are intended to be taken together as she is a 92 bis (D) witness. And specifically we cite to the jurisprudence that indicates exhibits attached to written statements or transcripts form an inseparable and indispensable part of the testimony. That was found in the Prosecution versus Naletilic and Martinovic cases, specifically 9834 PT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these two exhibits are accepted as part of the record in this case, but exactly under what provision will be determined when the Trial Chamber issues an order on various outstanding issues in relation to the admissibility of evidence, so that there's no doubt about the basis on which they are part of the record. It is rather -- I'm slightly confused by the reference to a package and then the transcript, but I follow what you're saying about what is generally regarded as included within a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, the 92 bis package, what is intended by that term is that it is the attestation as well as the original signed statement by the witness. As the witness does not sign off on the transcript, it's not considered part of the 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a different description from the one you earlier gave me, but that I can understand. But you understand you've given me two different descriptions of that, but I accept the latter one. You did already tell me that the transcript was part of the package. Anyway, we shall resolve it fairly soon and -- as far as the technicalities are concerned, and meanwhile we can concentrate on the merits. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, just for the record, if they are tendering this exhibit pursuant to 92 bis (D), my reading of that rule states that it cannot go towards acts and conduct of the accused, and therefore I would object based upon the case law we cited in our motion relating to As Seen, As Told, the appeals court decision, stating that acts and conduct of the accused includes alleged acts and conduct of alleged subordinate units, and so I don't think that that's an appropriate use of Rule 92 bis (D), if that's in fact what they are utilising to bring this in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you must have taken this point if you intended to use it, in response to the 92 bis application, and we must have dealt with it already if you took the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For some reason I don't recall that they sought to introduce this under 92 bis (D); I thought it was under another provision of 92 bis. But I could be mistaken. Perhaps I should bring that up outside of court if I review my pleadings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, what do you have to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
