utterances.text: Your Honour, this was tendered under Rule 92 bis (D) and a ruling has already taken place on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, because of the way this has developed today I may do some skipping around that I otherwise would not have done, and I hope for your indulgence in -- as I try to stumble through this process today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, good afternoon. My name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this case, and I have several questions that I'd like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As a -- as a very preliminary matter, you will find that we will get through this process much more easily if you will listen very carefully to the question I ask you and only answer that question and not go beyond the question that I ask you. Will you try to do that, please?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd appreciate that, and I think we all would. The first thing I want to ask you about is after you came here to The Hague, sometime within the last few days, you've had some meetings with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who are the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor that you met with to discuss this case and your testimony?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know the names of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet with the lawyer who's been asking you questions today?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you don't know her name?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. I forgot it. She told me her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet with any investigators?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the same time you met with Ms. Carter, the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you all meet together in a room and did this entire process occur within that one time in a room?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you and Ms. Carter and an investigator were there. Was there anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was a lady also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who was taking notes?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The lady that has been asking me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She was writing down the things you were telling her?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did she ask you why the things you were telling her were so different from the statement you had made earlier?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. I only told her things which I have gone through and experienced myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But she didn't ask you why you were making changes in the statements you had made earlier with the things you were telling her. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: What have I changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get into that in a little while and I'll show you what you've changed; it's quite a bit, I think, although I haven't had time to go through it in detail. Let me ask you this: Before you came here, did you have occasion to meet with any people who discussed the testimony you would give here with you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who would those people have been?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The people I told you about. Because my testimony is the same that I gave initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the people -- my question was not understood by you and that's my fault, not yours. Before you came to The Hague, before you came here, did you meet with people who you discussed your testimony with?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, no. This is what I'm saying. After I came here, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet with any other people of your nationality, any other Kosovo Albanians, to discuss your testimony before you came here?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't tell anyone my testimony, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to start by asking you about the 24th of March, 1999. That was the day the NATO bombing started, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on the 26th of March, you were in your home in Bukos, is it, Bukos, with your husband and your children?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. From Vushtrri we passed through Bukos but didn't go into our homes. We went to Kozhice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the places where what you told us today is different from your statement. In your statement in the second paragraph you told us that you lived in the village of Bukos. In the second paragraph you said to us: "Two days after the NATO bombs started last year, I left my home, my home, with my husband and my children and also my brother," and you name some other people. And you went to the village of Kozica. You said you did that on the 26th. Now today you're telling us something different. So that's one of the places where it's different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. On the 22nd of February we left our home. We went to visit it afterwards, but they did not allow us to enter home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what was you meant then in your statement when you said: "Two days after the NATO bombs started ... I left my home with my husband," what home were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. I said that we went to our home, but we didn't stay there. On the 26th, as I say, we returned from Vushtrri to my home and we left from my home to Kozhice, but we didn't stay at home. They didn't let us enter the home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. My point is --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: And you know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My point is you didn't say that in your statement; you said that for the first time today. You've added that. And you've either made it up or it's something you've remembered and I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I didn't add anything. I'm telling you how things were. We didn't dare enter the home. We went up to the yard. From Vushtrri we came there on the 26th, but we didn't dare stay there. And from my home we left for Kozhice. How can I say something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there is a third possibility, which I think you're going to have to bear in mind here, and that is that the statement was not terribly well recorded at the time it was first taken. You've given two possibilities, but I think there are more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you referring to the possibility that the statement was just unartfully done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that of course can happen. I've seen it before. But we're given these statements and we're given a 92 bis statement where the witness swears that everything in it is true. And when that happens, when we get the 92 bis statement saying I swear everything in there is true, then I think we can take it as -- not just for granted but take it as proof that what the witness is saying in there is what the witness intended to say. So I think it's no longer a statement that is unartfully done, I think it's virtual testimony, and that's why it comes in under 92 bis. So I think that's not a possibility in this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you would say that that was especially so where the witness has already given evidence before the Tribunal a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And adopted the statement then, too, and didn't tell the Milosevic Trial Chamber all these new things that have come in today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What a mess. Anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us today that -- let me do it this way. If one were to read your statement: "Two days after the NATO bombs started ... I left my home with my husband," one could conclude that it was because of the NATO bombing that you left your home. That would be a logical conclusion, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, we didn't leave because of NATO bombs but because of the shelling by the Serb forces of Vushtrri. And people got killed. That was a reason why, not because of NATO strikes. And I think you know this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know it very well because I wasn't there, but you were. And it's your information that we're trying to get, not mine. Now, in -- on a -- on 2nd of February, 1999, what village did you leave then? Was that -- was that your home, Bukos, was it Bukos you left on February 2nd?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: On the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm holding the proofing notes that were given me. It says on 2nd of February you, your children, and your sister left the village, I assume that's Bukos, and that the 2 is a mistake; it should be 22. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Correct. It should be 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you told the Prosecutor's office on Monday when you were being asked about these things was that you left because there was shooting in the area that you could hear. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told the Prosecutor that you were aware that there was military training going on in the neighbourhood at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor didn't ask you about that and you didn't tell us that when you started your testimony today, did you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: When you ask me, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you left the impression with this Trial Chamber, and I believe -- I suggest to you you intended to, that that shooting was against your village and against you when in fact it was a military exercise and you just heard the shots. And that's what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to this as being argumentive. The question was never asked. This witness could not have given an impression to this Chamber that a training exercise was taking place when she was never asked about any sort of training exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And to suggest that she intended to mislead this Court is wholly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that the witness said that: "There were bullets right up to the courtyard of my house."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Different -- different situation, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. All right. Well, did the witness give evidence that could be interpreted the way in which you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you will read the testimony the witness gave to the questions that were asked by the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to give me a reference and I'll go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's impossible for me to give you a reference because -- you'll know in a minute why I'm saying that. If you look at the testimony the witness gave, it was largely unresponsive to the questions. There would be a very brief answer to the question and then a four- or five- or six-line just statement about something else. So she was trying to give information beyond what she was being asked and she was doing so rather frequently. So to suggest that she didn't mention this because she wasn't asked is a bit disingenuous, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for a later stage. What I want to know at the moment is whether your characterisation of this particular piece of her evidence is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can assist my colleague. At the transcript page 14, they're talking about the -- at line 20 through 25 the Prosecutor and the witness are talking about the 22nd of February, and the insinuation there is that there was shelling in the mountains of Taraxh and the children were scared. "When you can say 'the army,' can you describe who was shelling those villages?" So I believe that there was definitely evidence led and inference made that the actions on that date involved shelling of villages. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, does your question relate to the 22nd of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, again, for clarification of the record, if counsel would then refer to page 15 following this entire train of thought it indicates question on line 8 -- or excuse me, on line 7: "At what time was -- were the bullets in your courtyard?" Line 8: "It was 2.00 p.m. while two days after my husband and my brother-in-law, Bajram, were told by the army to leave the house because otherwise they will be killed." It's very clear what -- that she was referring to a specific instance in time. A date as not provided -- well, actually, a date was provided later in regards to the 22nd. Again, we initiate -- or excuse me. We renew our objection that to indicate that this witness was somehow being misleading is wholly inappropriate. She gave the evidence very clearly about what took place on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, the description -- the passage to which Mr. Ivetic has drawn attention is exactly the same one as I mentioned which you've told me related to a different event. I'm not satisfied that the evidence has been characterised correctly in the question you've asked, and therefore you'll have to approach this matter in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have a further objection, Your Honour, and that's this: The -- the responsibilities of a Prosecutor are not just to seek a conviction but to do justice. And if we had not been given these proofing notes, you would have never heard that she said that the shooting that she heard in her area on that day was a result of military training, not an attack on her village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not in the business of trying to act as a boxing referee between two parties who want to have the last word. I've made my ruling, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you left your village, your home on February 22nd, I think it's your testimony today that you went to Vucitrn. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how far is it from Bukos to Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Some three kilometres, I think. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could it be less than that? Is it likely that it's less than that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It could. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that -- that all of these villages you've talked about, Vucitrn, Bukos, Kozica, Cirez, all of these villages are all within two kilometres of each other, aren't they? They're in an area -- a two-kilometre area. They're all right next to each other.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. From Bukos to Vushtrri is a bit farther. For the others I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They're very close, though, aren't they? It's not like you were going all over the country.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, they're not close. There is, I think, more than -- over 10 kilometres to Vushtrri from Cirez.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if I knew more about the system here, I probably could bring up a map and have you look at it. I think it will probably show that it's close, but I don't know. In your conversations with the Prosecution, you told the Prosecutor that many Serbs lived in our village. Would that be the village of Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told the Prosecutor that two Serbs died a few days prior to the NATO bombing. Now, when you say "two Serbs died," what did they die of?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I heard it on the television. I wasn't really interested personally in what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't hear that they died of natural causes. You heard that they were killed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We heard that they died from the television. I don't know what they died of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why -- if they just died of old age, why was it relevant to put that in your statement? You put it in there because they were killed and you later explain why that's significant, and we'll get to that. But you know that they didn't just die of old age. You know that they were killed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I was just interested in my family and my children. I don't know what other -- what happened to other people. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, many more than two people die every day in Kosovo. The fact that two people die is of no consequence. This is mentioned in your statement clearly because it is of some significance to the case. And Mr. Ackerman is only rightly asking you to tell him your full knowledge of this event. So please tell him what you know about the death of these two Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard about it from the television that they'd been killed. But I don't know exactly what happened. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you'll recall that I'd asked you three times. They'd been killed, hasn't they, and you said you didn't know. Now when the Judge intervenes you all of a sudden say, yes, they were killed. Why does that happen? You're here under oath, you know.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I'm just telling you I heard about it on television. I don't know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't even ask you if you knew personally -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Rrahmani, can you tell me on which television you learned of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what are the possibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've forgotten. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what television stations at that time were you able to watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was the men who watched television, and they told us what was going on around, in the village and elsewhere, in Bukos and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, I want to remind you of something. When you walked into this courtroom today before you started your testimony you said to this Chamber, I believe, these words: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm just telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you you're not. You just told the Judge when he asked you about what television station -- let me finish - what television station you saw this on that it really wasn't you who saw it, the men watched the television and you were told. But on line -- at page 56, line 2 of the transcript, your testimony is: "I heard it on television." Now, when you say: "I heard it on television," you're telling us you heard it on television, and that now you're telling us was not true and not the truth and not the oath you took before this Chamber. Explain that.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We heard about it, but the -- we heard about it from the television, and it was the men who told us that it was in Bukos because we didn't know that. That was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say: "We heard about it on the television," you're not including you, are you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I was -- I heard about it, but I don't know the names of the people there, their first names or their last names. The men know. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're really not answering my questions, Ms. Rrahmani --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It's not that I'm not trying to tell you the truth --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and you're not answering properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. There's an objection being taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would object to this as being argumentive. This witness has been very clear. She said repeatedly her husband and the other men heard this on TV; they told the women. This is becoming a debate about semantics and is wholly argumentative. And also the questions being posed to this witness are multifarious. We would ask very clear and distinct questions be asked of this witness so that she might answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example of what you describe as a multifarious question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Page 58, starting at line 1: "Well, I suggest to you you're not. You just told the Judge when he asked you about the television station -- let me finish - what television you saw this on ... It really wasn't me who saw it, the men watched the television ... You were told" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is requested to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Within that sentence, he is attempting to take this witness first through a transcript that she can't read. He is bringing in multiple aspects of her testimony. This witness is attempting to answer his questions to the best of her ability. When she says she doesn't know, that is not an acceptable answer. When she does try to explain, if she doesn't explain in the proper semantics, that is not considered an answer by this counsel. So I would urge the Court to find this to be argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The questions in my opinion are entirely focussed. The point is a justified one to challenge because the witness has given two clearly contradictory accounts and she should have the opportunity to clarify that. I repel your objection. Please carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to move beyond this. I think it's been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I love this e-court system, Your Honour, it just told me that my computer's been locked. All right. It's back now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This same paragraph that I was talking about from your -- your meetings with the Prosecutor where you talked about two Serbs dying a few days prior to the NATO bombing, you told the Prosecutor that prior to the NATO bombing one of the Serbian neighbours said - and you heard that one of the Serbian neighbours said that to be fair to you - that if the KLA attacks us, everyone in the village will get killed. So there was a concern, was there not, that because of what had happened in that village that the KLA might attack the village.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said. We -- the Serbs were killed. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so when you told this Chamber a few moments ago that on 26th March, 1999 you left your village because you were afraid for your family, you and your family's safety, what you were afraid of was an attack from the KLA, wasn't it, not from anything Serbs were doing?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. We never -- we were never afraid of the KLA. They came and they -- they removed us from our houses. We were never afraid of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told the Prosecutor that you were told that if the KLA attacked everyone in the village would get killed, that didn't -- that didn't cause you any fear, that everyone in the village would get killed if the KLA came and attacked? You weren't afraid of that? Is that what you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We were afraid of the Serbs, that's why we left and went away. Not from the KLA, because in Bukos village there were no KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There had been KLA there before, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see them. I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That comment that's been recorded is clearly open to a different interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say: "You heard" -- this is the problem. It wasn't the notes I expected to be disclosed to you, it was the information that was relevant from the notes. But if the KLA attacks everyone in the village will get killed, that's equally open to the interpretation that it's a threat, and that's what the witness is trying to say to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean that it's a threat? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the KLA attack the Serbs in the village, then there will be retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Everyone will be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, it's open to that interpretation, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's what the witness is trying to say to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you left wherever it was you were, Vucitrn I guess, on the 26th, you then went to the village of Kozica. And I think that's about 500 metres away, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: You mean from Vushtrri to Kozica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's about 500 metres, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, no. It's farther than that, not 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: From Vucitrn to Kozhice, the distance is greater. Maybe from Kozica to Cirez it may be as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've just been told that I was in error on that and that it is between Kozica and Cirez that it's 500 metres and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the village of Kozica, there were KLA there when you arrived there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone from KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were there for about three days when you encountered what I will term the first group of soldiers who you say arrived and shelled the village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see the weapons that were being used to shell the village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: When they came there they came with tanks, and I saw the shells -- the grenades being fired at the houses. In the courtyard, before going to Rrahim's house, we saw the grenade falling before our very eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say "grenade," is that something that's being thrown by hand, or is that a shell that's being fired by a gun, or what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: For me a grenade is a big shell, or long thing over some metres fired from a tank. And I saw it with my own eyes. Maybe you have another name for it, but I refer to it as grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That clarifies it. That's good enough. Thank you. Now, as a result of this shelling a couple of things happened. Some people were killed and some people were wounded. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the men from that village left the village and went into the mountains, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how were they able to get out of the village and go into the mountains without being seen by these soldiers who were close to the village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Maybe they saw them and they fired at them, but my husband was lucky and my brother-in-law were lucky to escape. Maybe some got killed. I don't know. The only thing I know is that men left because they couldn't dare stay -- remain there because they would be killed. They went to Cicavica. They fired at the group of women and children, let alone at the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you -- your husband didn't tell you that they had killed any of the men, did he? You have no information that any of the men that left that village had been killed, do you, that day?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I have no information that someone was killed that day, with the exception of that young man that was shot who was with our group. I cannot tell you about things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, and I'm talking about the men who left the village and went to the mountains. None of those men were killed. They apparently got away safely. And as far as you know, no one chased them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Cicavica is very near to Kozica. Maybe they couldn't see them, because from the house we were staying, Xhemajl Xhema's, from there to Cicavica mountain is very close, maybe some five [Realtime transcript read in error "500"] metres away. So once the shelling started, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The transcript says -- 500 metres to Cicavica, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Five metres. I said five metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's 15 feet or -- I mean, nobody knows what that means. That's very close. That's like the distance between you and me.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It is. I know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you were in Vucitrn, I would be in Cicavica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. From the house of Xhemajl where we were staying, Cicavica is very close, next to the house, from that house, not from Vushtrri. We got together, all the women, at Rrahim's house, where the men -- whereas the men left for Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Cicavica was a well-known KLA stronghold, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the men went into the mountains because they were afraid they might have -- they might get killed. I don't know how they remained alive there because they had nothing to eat and to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Once these soldiers actually arrived into the village after there had been shelling, they sought to give treatment to the wounded people that were there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. There were ten dead, three injured, from Gjakova. They tied their wounds. They did a good job, those three people that were wounded, and then they asked us to sit down in that yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've answered my question and I appreciate that. I think there was a doctor with them, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they -- they first checked to make sure there were no armed men or anybody with arms in that village, that there were no KLA there hiding in any of the houses, and then they started to treat the people that had been injured. That's a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. They set the houses on fire, and then after that they came and tied the wounds of the injured. They took us to a room, to oda, and told us to give them everything valuable we had on us. They got everything we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You left Kozica then and you went to -- I think you said in your statement that you went to Glogovac. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Skenderaj. They didn't let us enter Skenderaj. Then we moved on to Gllogoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you stayed there for ten days in the house of your husband's uncle. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you went back to Kozica --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- the place where you had encountered these soldiers, you went back there because you had no food. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that you could get food in Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We wanted to ask people who were there to lend us some flour or anything, something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you got back there, your husband and the other men who had fled to the mountains had come back, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't have anything to eat in Cicavica, and they came indeed when dusk fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you stayed -- started staying in Xhafer Daka's house in Kozica until around the middle of April, when again some shots were heard, some shelling was heard, and your husband and the other men went back to the mountains. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's when the boy came and said that you would be better off if you went to Durmishi's house, and so you went there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there you encountered a second group of soldiers, was it, different from the ones you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They checked you for weapons, and then after they found you had no weapons --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. They searched us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After they found you had no weapons, they then treated you very well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. For three days at Durmishi's house my daughter was running a high temperature, and they gave me some medicine. But after three days when they took us to Cirez, they killed the mother and the daughters, those girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, not those same soldiers. That's not your testimony.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These soldiers, when you were at Durmishi's house, they got food for you, they got dry clothes for you, right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you concluded that they must have been regular Yugoslav army because not only the uniforms they were wearing but the kindness with which they treated you. True?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you were -- a soldier came and said that you must get ready to go to Cirez. And these soldiers who had been treating you so well escorted you over to Cirez, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were treated very well on that walk, nothing bad happened to anyone, right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during this walk you learned that they were moving you for your own safety because they said they were expecting an offensive in Kozica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: This is what they told us, but this didn't turn out to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, where is it you're getting -- what's the basis for these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The statement we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Cirez, you encountered a completely different kind of people. They were older men. They were dressed in these brown and black uniforms. One of them had five stars on his shoulder. They had -- some of them had beards, I believe, long hair, right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in fact I think someone suggested to you later that they may have been members of the Black Hand, a paramilitary group, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as you've told this Chamber, that group of men were brutal and horrible and did not treat you or any of your companions well at all, did they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: That's right. This is what I told them, and this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. After a time, one of these soldiers then came to you, one of these Black Hand paramilitary guys, said you should go back to Durmishi's house in Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. After they searched every one of us, after they took away the five girls, three women, then a soldier came in and said: Go back to Kozica where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, please understand that we acknowledge that those horrible things happened to you there at the hands of these Black Hand people and we're very sorry those happened to you. Please understand that. Had you heard of this Black Hand before that day, before you learned about who -- that's who they might be?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In Likoshane village, I heard a year ago, after some bad things happened in a family in Likoshane, they killed a pregnant woman and so on, I heard -- that was a time when I heard for the first time that these were done by the Black Hand, but before that I knew nothing of the Black Hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you went back to Cirez and saw the soldiers that you had seen there before, you felt comfortable enough about your relationship with them to tell them about what had happened to you in Cirez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in fact they expressed a great deal of concern and sympathy for your situation and what had happened to you there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: This is what they told us. But when we went to Kozica I saw again the same soldier. He knew what happened. But they behaved well with us even though they knew very well where they were taking us. Because when we returned to Kozica again, before entering Durmishi's house, it was one house some 50 metres away, I saw the soldier that took us to Cirez and I said to this my group, to the group of people, and I pin-pointed at him because I couldn't speak in Serbo-Croatian. When he saw me pin-pointing at him, he went inside because he was afraid lest we would go up to him and tell him: Why did you take us there? What are you doing to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, look at 69, line 9, when you went back to -- should that be Kozica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it should be Cirez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll clear that up just so that there's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you had gone back to Kozica and told the soldiers about what had happened there in Cirez, they took you back to Cirez to try to help you find the missing women and girls, didn't they? That's what they said they were going to do, find out what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: When they -- after they took away the girls and told us to go to Kozhice, this is when I saw the soldier. Before we entered the Durmishi's house. And I told the people in my group: This is the soldier that escorted us to Cirez. But as I said when he saw me pointing at him, he went inside and didn't leave the house until we passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've already told us that about three times now, but that's not the question I asked you. When you explained to the soldiers back in Kozica what had happened in Cirez, they went back there with you to try to find out what had happened to the missing women and girls? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, they came with us. But when I showed them that this is the barn when they took away the girls, they told me: Go ahead. I know, I know. And they moved us further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You went then to a different house in Cirez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in that house you encountered yet another group, what I call a fourth group of soldiers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these soldiers also treated you well. They brought you food and flour to bake bread?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say what they didn't do. I am just saying what they did, what happened to us. I told you that they behaved well in Kozhice and again when they sent us to Cirez. Maybe among them there were also good people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, just to be fair with both you and the Chamber, while you were in this second place in Cirez, the house where they brought you food and flour and so forth and treated you well, you did say that two soldiers came at one point and demanded some money. But in your statement you said that this was probably not known to the other soldiers, that those two soldiers were operating on their own without permission, basically. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. Because as I said, they had behaved well, but then two soldiers came inside and they asked us to give them money. We pulled together some 400 Deutschmarks, and they said: If you don't -- your group doesn't give us 200 Deutschmarks, you will get killed. And they turned to Hajrije and asked her for money, and she said: I have no money. And he brought out his arm and shot in the air just to scare us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next thing that happened, the next move, these soldiers came and told you that you should go to Glogovac because they believed there was going to be an offensive in Cirez and you would be safe in Glogovac. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, is this a suitable time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll adjourn now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, I want to take you back in time to those days in the fall of the year 2000 when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. There was an interviewer there by the name of Annette Murtagh and a couple of interpreters that worked with her on that day. Do you remember -- actually, it was three days. Do you remember that three-day period when you were giving your original statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things I'm sure they did was give you an opportunity to just tell your story without asking a bunch of questions but just have you tell the story and tell them what happened and tell them the important things that you believed happened during these times. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then after -- after this three-day period, they actually created a witness statement, and before you finished they read that out to you and it was translated into your language. And you acknowledged that it was true and signed it and basically signed every page of it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were given -- they gave you every opportunity to tell them everything you could remember that you thought was significant about these days in your life. Correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you testified today you talked about -- it's -- it's hard to tell, Your Honour, because I have a print-out. I think it's page 22 of the transcript. In any event, you were talking about when that first group of soldiers came to the village where you were where the tanks you said were firing -- shelling the village. You told us today that there was this mentally disabled young man 30 years old, 28 years old, who was shouting and crying. And you said: They shot him immediately right then and there in the Kozica village in this house. That's what you told us today, right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I can't find that anywhere in the statement that you spent three days giving to the Prosecutor in the year 2000 where you were given plenty of time to tell them everything that was significant that you could remember. Do you think you told them that at the time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell them about that. I forgot to tell them, but I mentioned it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to a little bit later in your testimony today. I think it's on page 29 of the transcript. You were talking about the time that you were going I believe from Cirez to -- to Glogovac, and you saw trucks on the road containing soldiers. And you said this. You said: "You could only see women and children. There were no men because if they found men there, they would kill them immediately, even young boys, 13 years old, they would kill them." Now, you never saw any of these soldiers kill young boys 13 years old, did you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked a great deal over and over I might say, about what colour uniforms people were wearing, the soldiers you were seeing. And you talked -- you were asked about green uniforms and camouflage green uniforms and brown and black uniforms, and I don't know how many other colours of uniforms. You can't, by looking at the colour of a uniform someone's wearing, tell what unit they're from or what service they're from or anything else, can you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I said green. This is what I call in our language in the village. We call them green.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this is a matter for comment. It's not a question that the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And she hasn't endeavoured to make the link in any event, has she?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave it alone, Your Honour. Wise advice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have just one more question. At the -- near the end of your statement to the Prosecutor, after you had been the second time in Cirez for three weeks and you were told that you should go to Glogovac because there was going to be an offensive in Cirez, the soldiers believed that where do you might be in danger there and suggested you go to Glogovac. And what you said was: "And we went to Glogovac and we would get buses to Macedonia." Now, today what you said, and this is page 42, starting with line 9, you were asked: "After the three weeks in Cirez, where did you go next?" "A. They told us that you will go to Glogovac," it says here Gllogoc, "and we will send you to Macedonia" --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- "There's no place for you here." Now, that's entirely different from what you said in your statement. In your statement the indication is they were sending you there for your safety, and that's what's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There were 11 buses sent towards that direction, and people said that some of the buses were stopped and people were told to get down. I know that these buses were loaded with people and drove to -- in the direction of Macedonia. But I don't know where they went exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've totally misunderstood my question, and again that's probably my fault. The indication in your statement -- in fact, you say directly in your statement that you were told by the soldiers that you were being sent to Glogovac because there was going to be an offensive in Cirez, they believed, and it would be dangerous for you to stay there. That's what you said in your statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Not that. In Cirez they said it's because of that. But when the buses came close to Gllogoc they said: This is not your place. You have to leave. Go to Macedonia. But where we were before, in Cirez, we were told: It's better for you to go somewhere else because it's dangerous for you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. That makes total sense because the people that -- after you got on the buses and got over to Glogovac the people who told you what they told you there are not these soldiers who were trying to get you to safety out of Cirez but a different group, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They had the same uniform, but I don't know if they were the same or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for answering my questions, I appreciate it. And I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, can you tell me whether the basis for the question that led to the answer which you were characterising as being contradictory of what is in that third-last paragraph of the statement, whether that information is in the proofing notes you were given, or is that something which has come spontaneously in the evidence today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's in the proofing notes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I don't see it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've agreed to proceed in the following order after counsel for General Pavkovic: Counsel for Mr. Milutinovic, counsel for Mr. Sainovic, counsel for General Ojdanic, General Lazarevic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In other words, according to the indictment, so carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila -- sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may inquire, if we can have a rough estimate from the Defence whether remaining cross-examine will take us until 7.00 because I think we have the next witness waiting here who could return early to the hotel if we're not going to get to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Hannis, I'll check that in a moment. Mr. Fila, your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- oh, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- sorry, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have some questions for this witness, and I anticipate if everything goes the way I've anticipated about 30 minutes worth of questions, so that would leave about 15 minutes in this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the witness should return to the hotel, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Rrahmani. My name is Dan Ivetic, and along with my colleague here, Mr. Branko Lukic, and our case manager, Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic, today I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic. And I have to ask you for your patience because we have some questions that we have to ask you regarding what you witnessed in Kosovo-Metohija to clear up a few things that you may have already testified to. Now, my first question relates to the time period of March 1999, and in your written statement at -- in the Albanian it's page 2, paragraph 3, and I believe that it is the same citation for all three versions of the transcript. You make reference to the fact that the NATO bombs started in March of 1999, and my first question for you would be: Is it thus accurate to state that NATO planes were flying overhead, that is to say over the municipality of Vucitrn and over the villages that you have described here today in March of 1999 on a very frequent basis?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Whose airplanes you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: NATO.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: You mean before the 26th of March? I did not understand the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- allow me to rephrase the question. After March the 24th of 1999, I believe you had indicated that the NATO bombs had started to -- the NATO bombs had started, is I believe what you said. I'm asking you for that time period after that date, is it a fair statement to state that NATO planes frequently flew overhead over the Vucitrn municipality, including the several villages within that municipality that we have discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I did not see any. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to clear up a few matters, the village where you -- where your home is, that's Bukos village. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how big is Bukos village in terms of population?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is Bukos small enough to permit you to at least be acquainted with most of the people who live there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know all the people. It's quite a large village. It's a large village, but I don't know how many inhabitants it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I believe that you stated that there were many Serbs that lived in Bukos. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have knowledge that some of these Serb families began leaving Bukos during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There were two families that were living close to us, and they were there all the time. I don't know about other people who might have been living farther away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. Well, during the time period of 1998 and 1999, isn't it a fact that some of these Serb families were -- were receiving threats from the so-called UCK-KLA in Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. Until the moment those two Serbs were killed, I had never heard that anybody had been threatened by the KLA. I don't know who killed those two Serbs. I'm not sure, but that's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, ma'am, prior to living in Bukos village you were born in a village called Dubovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: It's called Dubovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the Albanian it's Dobovc. In Serbian is that Dubovac?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1999 did you still have friends and/or family that lived in Dubovc?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. When I was a child, I cannot remember -- I don't remember that there were any Serbs in that village when I was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, perhaps my question wasn't -- wasn't clear. In 1999, did you still have any friends or family that lived in Dubovc?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And -- first of all, as far as Bukos is concerned, did you have knowledge of any so-called UCK or KLA that were present in that village at any time during 1998 through 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There might have been, but I haven't seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how about for your birth village of Dubovc?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. There might have been, but I didn't see any. I went to visit for a couple of hours, went back to my children. I did not stay there for such a long time to see who was in the village. I told you, there might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, isn't it true that the UCK or KLA, as they called themselves, were engaged in acts of violence within Bukos village, specifically during early 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing about this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, I believe earlier today you testified about two Serbs that were killed. If I can ask you to focus in on that. I believe that the -- that you -- well, strike that. Mr. Ackerman asked you, my colleague Mr. Ackerman asked you whether in fact you left your village due to the attacks upon these Serb civilians. And I believe he asked you about March of 1999. I want to ask you about February of 1999, specifically February 22nd, 1999, when you testified that you left your home in Bukos village for the first time. Isn't it a fact that on February 22nd of 1999 there was a shooting that took place in Bukos village where the UCK-KLA killed one Serbian civilian, wounded two other civilians, and that this was a widely reported incident. Do you have a recollection of that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I know -- I don't know who shot into my courtyard. We left our house because of all the shooting. It was the Serbian army who shot at our houses. There are other things that are not in my statement here that I could add. My relatives were forced out of their house with automatic rifles at their throats and forced --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm talking about February 22nd specifically, and specifically about an event that was recorded, and I believe this is the event that you saw on TV relating to the attack by the UCK-KLA upon Serbian residents of Bukos village, Mr. Milan Milosevic, Mr. Milos Prodanovic, and Mr. Mirko Milosevic. Is that not in fact true that this attack occurred on the very same day that you claim that you left your village, on February 22nd of 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know whether the KLA killed them. I just saw on television that people were killed, but I don't know who they were. I had just heard that they were from Bukos.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact I believe you testified earlier today that you didn't really pay attention to what was on the TV. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I didn't know what they were saying because of the language, and my husband explained to me that it was an incident in our village of Bukos.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, more than that, isn't it a fact that prior to -- prior to returning to Bukos and engaging in the act that resulted in the death of one person and the wounding of two others, that this incident also took place in Dubovc, your birth village, that is to say that the KLA kidnapped these people and took them to your birth village, then brought them back to the village you lived in and shot them. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know who killed them. I just know what I heard at the time. I don't know who they were. My husband told me that it had happened in the village of Bukos. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just confused why you would not be more interested in such an event that included the village you lived in as well as your birth village and killings. I would think that that would be a very -- very concerning fact to be made aware of. Were you not at all concerned about what had transpired?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Well, we heard about it, as I said, from the news, and it had happened a day earlier than that. And we stayed in the village even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after that event, that is to say after the incident of February 22nd, 1999, the killing of Mr. Mirko Milosevic, isn't it a fact that the Serbian police accompanied by the OSCE-KVM mission came to Bukos village and that they, too, were fired upon by the KLA. Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Are you saying that they shot against the OSCE? I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Isn't it a fact that the following day after this incident that we discussed, the Serbian police and the OSCE-KVM mission came to your village of Bukos to investigate the shooting, and that on that second day the KLA, using mortars and infantry weapons, shot upon the Serbian police, first of all, wounding five police officers and one reporter from the Associated Press. And then after that shot upon the OSCE vehicle that was in Bukos village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, isn't it a fact that on the night you claim you left Bukos village, the 22nd of February, isn't it a fact that you testified in the Milosevic proceedings at page 4584 of the transcript, lines 18 through 25, and I quote the question. "It happened on the 22nd of February, the killing of those two young men, and the villagers on the next day, that is to say the Kosovo Verification Mission, was there the next day and the KLA shot at members of the mission, too. Do you remember that? Did you hear the shooting on -- in your village at all, both on the 22nd and on the 23rd of February?" And your answer was: "On the 22nd of February in the evening, we left the house because there was fighting in the village and there were forces there, but we didn't know what was going on." My question to you is: Did you in fact leave your village of Bukos on the 22nd of February because of the activity of the KLA against these -- these parties that I've identified, first on the 22nd against civilians, and then on the 23rd against the Serbian police, the Associated Press reporter, and the OSCE. Was that not the real reason you left on the 22nd of February, the chaos that was ensuing due to a KLA attack?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We did not know who was shooting against whom that day. We left with the children. The men were staying there, but the next day the men were forced to leave the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you: After that date, isn't it a fact that many ethnic Albanians remained in Bukos village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: People who were living close to where I was living left. I don't know about people further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Hamil Pllana who was a resident of Bukos village in 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Hamil Pllana, no, I don't know him. I have never heard before of this name, Hamil.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know that on April 4th, 1999, it was reported that this individual, an ethnic Albanian, was killed by the KLA in your village of Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: He might have been killed. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it general knowledge within the area that you lived in that the so-called UCK or KLA was involved in violent attacks, both against Serb civilians and against Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Our houses were not attacked. I don't know about other people and other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of any acts of violent retaliation by the UCK-KLA against ethnic Albanian residents of Kosovo who cooperated with the Serbian government or rejected the militant path of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Maybe they attacked them. I'm not denying it, but the fact is that I don't know. But even if they attacked them, I think it serves them right, because why should they spy on us? Why should they give information to the enemy when we were being killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take that to mean, ma'am, that you have a negative impression of ethnic Albanians who reject the militant path of the KLA and choose to cooperate with the state that they live in?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They were killing us all, and you are talking just about one person who was killed. And things, what you are mentioning here, they might have happened, yes, but it's because of them that we were killed, because of the people who were spying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there a back-lash against these Albanians that followed the laws of the Serbian state and cooperated with the laws of the Serbian state on the part of the remaining Kosovo Albanian residents in your area, since I think that's probably the only place I can fairly ask you about?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I've exhausted all the questions that I have a little bit earlier than I had anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. I just want to bring to the Court's attention that there was some discussion during my case in chief in regards to what took place on February 22nd of 1999. What became an issue was this witness giving new information or something that the Defence counsel did not previously have. As has been clearly pointed out by Mr. Lukic today, February 22nd was at issue, February 22nd was in documents that Defence counsel had in their possession. It was the mistake of this counsel for indicating that it was first learned in proofing. However, the Defence counsel cannot claim surprise because it is a part of the submissions from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's Mr. Ivetic I think you're referring to. Which was the page in the transcript again? He referred to a reference to the 22nd of February in the Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. It's on page 4584, the question begins on page 18. Mr. Milosevic is trying to indicate that there was some KLA fighting in the village at that time. The witness then indicates: "We left the house because there was fighting in the village and there were forces there but we didn't know what was going on."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this in the way of re-direct? I didn't realise this issue was still pending?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, it's a clarification of our earlier discussion about -- at least it's an amplification of the Prosecution position on the earlier discussion we had about what may or may not have been disclosed. Now, do you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no further questions. I just wanted to bring that note to the Court's attention in an effort to show that we aren't being transparent and have provided all information that we had at our finger-tips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I find unfortunate is that in the light of a witness giving evidence, no steps are taken to pull all the material together and go over it with the witness in the pre-trial phase. I've tried very hard, as you know, to have that done. I failed abysmally in my efforts to do so. But I think that one of the lessons we've learned now with two witnesses in this case is that it actually works against the interests of the witness not to have done this. It means that a witness might feel that in one case his position has not been properly represented, and in another case might feel unjustly challenged because of the way in which the material has been gathered and presented. Having said that, we recognise we have to make what we can of what we receive, and that we will do. But it's not too late to argue yet again, if you can, to try to speak to the witnesses earlier and give everyone the final version, the updated final version at the earliest possible opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And I do hope that you'll not disappoint my Lord Bonomy on that, because it will help a lot because many things then we are looking and asking and then we're trying to cover and it leads to a sort of a skirmish, isn't it, sometimes, though politely, but I hope you will not disappoint my Lord again or the Bench. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rrahmani, that brings your evidence to an end. I hope that this is the last time that you have to come here, and I expect it will be. But thank you very much for coming again to The Hague to give your evidence, and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just checking that the possibility of sitting in the morning hasn't arisen tomorrow, but it hasn't as far as I have been able to check. So we will adjourn now and resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.40 p.m.,
